title: Vayikra: salt on every offering (Leviticus 2:13)
hookLine: "the salt of the covenant" on every offering, still sprinkled on bread today

cards: Friday night, in Jewish homes that keep the custom: after the blessing over the challah, the person cutting the bread sprinkles a little salt on it, or dips the piece into salt. It takes two seconds.
Kids sometimes fight over who gets the saltiest piece. But that pinch of salt goes all the way back to a single verse in this week's portion, and to an altar that stood in Jerusalem long ago.

teach.b: Here's the verse: "And every meal-offering of thine shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meal-offering; with all thy offerings thou shalt offer salt."
Just two verses earlier, the Torah forbids leaven and honey on the altar. No rising, no sweetening. But salt, always.

The text calls it the salt of the covenant, and elsewhere the Torah speaks of a covenant of salt that lasts forever. Salt doesn't rot; it preserves. Readers have heard in it a promise that doesn't go bad.

teach.h: THE SEA'S PLACE ON THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Rashi takes the covenant back to creation: when God divided the waters, the lower waters, the seas, were promised a place on the altar, in the salt that comes from the sea, and in the water poured there on Sukkot.
Other midrashim add that the lower waters wept at being sent far from God. The farthest waters get to come near. And the bread?
The Talmud says that while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement; now that it's gone, a person's table does.
Later authorities drew the line from there: if the table is like the altar, the bread on it gets salt, like every offering. A pinch of salt on Friday night is an altar remembered in a kitchen.

how: Jews who keep the custom sprinkle salt on bread or dip it in salt after saying the blessing over it, especially on Shabbat, recalling that the table stands in place of the altar.

o: and He rested: words from the seventh day
and He divided: the waters at creation
and He called: the first word of the book

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: promised a place on the altar
stands in place of the altar

s: salt was put on only some offerings
with all thy offerings thou shalt offer salt.
honey was offered on the altar for sweetness
the Torah forbids leaven and honey on the altar, two verses before the salt.
the custom of salting bread links the table to the altar
the Talmud says that now a person's table brings atonement, as the altar did.

games.q: you're preparing a grain offering. the Torah has just forbidden leaven and honey on the altar. what must you add to every offering?
games.why: salt, on every offering: the salt of the covenant, which doesn't spoil.

practice: If you can, take a small piece of bread or a cracker and a pinch of salt; if not, just picture it.
Sprinkle the salt slowly, and think of one promise in your life that has kept: a friendship that didn't spoil, a commitment someone kept to you, or one you've kept.
Taste the salt, or imagine it, and let it stand for everything that lasts.

wordCard.voice: Vayikra. And He called. The book that commands salt on every offering: the salt of the covenant.

orig.note: Hebrew: the salt of the covenant, from Leviticus 2:13.

carryVoice: Your line: salt of the covenant. Some promises don't spoil. Three hundred eighty-three days now.
